Midquarter Report - Gursajan Gill

1.  **Refined Question:** What are the spike dynamics of auditory-responsive neurons? Can auditory-responsive neurons be classified into different subtypes based on their spike dynamics?
2.  **Description of Data:** This dataset is collected by me using a Neuropixels 2.0 probe that I inserted into the brain of an awake and behaving mouse and presented 100ms-long auditory stimuli to the mouse. Before making these .csv files, I used a program called Kilosort4 to take the continuous voltage output of the Neuropixels 2.0 probe and turned it into discrete spike times. Kilosort4 spit out three different .csv files in this dataset:
    1.  cluster_info.csv (100 KB) - this file contains 482 rows. Each row is a separate "cluster" that potentially can be a neuron. Kilosort4 gives each cluster a label: "good" for clusters that look like a good single-unit neuron; "mua" for clusters that look like multiple neurons that can not be resolved individually; "noise" for clusters that are simply noise or not neuronal activity. As is typical in Neuropixels recordings, I will only look at the "good" neurons.
    2.  "spikes_seg2_speaker_array_sound.csv" (111 MB) - this large file contains every single spike time for ever cluster. It has over 7 million rows because spikes for "good", "noisy" and "mua" neurons are all listed here. I will clean this up to only have the "good" neurons represented.
    3.  "trials.csv" (100 KB) - this file just shows the time when a sound played. There were 1170 trials in this recording, I will align the spike of each cluster from the spikes csv to find the clusters that are auditory-responsive.
3.  **Data Cleaning:** The main cleaning step I did is to keep only the "good" clusters in both the spikes csv and the cluster_info csv. In the spikes and trials csv I checked for any missing values and "NAs" (there were none):

```{r}
clusters <- read.csv("project_data/cluster_info.csv")
trials <- read.csv("project_data/trials.csv")
spikes <-read.csv("project_data/spikes_seg2_speaker_array_sound.csv")
clusters_good <- clusters[clusters$group == "good", ]
spikes_good <- spikes[spikes$unit %in% clusters_good$cluster_id, ]

nrow(clusters_good) # number of good clusters
nrow(spikes_good) # number of spikes from good clusters

sum(is.na(spikes_good)) # NA's and missing values from spikes_good
sum(is.na(trials)) # NA's and missing values from spikes_good
```

4.  **Figure 1:** This histogram describes the firing of the good clusters right after the 100ms stimulus onset (time zero)...we can see a clear population trend of good neurons having high firing rate right after a stimulus is turned on vs their spontaneous activity (the baseline levels the neuron returns to after stimulus offset).

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
clusters <- read.csv("project_data/cluster_info.csv")
trials <- read.csv("project_data/trials.csv")
spikes <-read.csv("project_data/spikes_seg2_speaker_array_sound.csv")
clusters_good <- clusters[clusters$group == "good", ]
spikes_good <- spikes[spikes$unit %in% clusters_good$cluster_id, ]

relative_spikes <- c() 
for (i in 1:1170) { # for loop to run for every trial "i" from trial 1 to trial 1170
trial_onset  <- trials$ttl_time_s[i] # onset time of trial
responsive_spike <- spikes_good$time_s >= trial_onset & spikes_good$time_s < trial_onset + 1.0 #sets spike as true if spike is after trial_onset and before trial_offset (each trial lasts 1000ms, the first 100ms is the stimulus)
relative_spikes  <- c(relative_spikes, (spikes_good$time_s[responsive_spike] - trial_onset) * 1000)} #the time of the spike relative to onset in ms

relative_spikes <- data.frame(time_ms = relative_spikes) #turn relative_spikes vector into a dataframe

ggplot(relative_spikes, aes(x = time_ms)) +
geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) + #plot histogram with 5ms bin width
labs(x = "Time After Stimulus Onset (ms)", y = "Number of Spikes", title = "# of Spikes of Clusters Post Stimulus Onset") +
theme_minimal() 
```

![](images/paste-2.png)

5.  **Figure 2:** Good vs MUA vs Noise spikes. This geom_point plots three lines, showing just the responsiveness of all clusters based on their type relative to trial_onset. This sanity check should show that good clusters should have the strongest auditory responsive component compared to MUA and especially compared to "noise" clusters. Here to make this plot, I binned the number of spikes into 5ms bins per cluster to allow for comparison across the three types.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
clusters <- read.csv("project_data/cluster_info.csv")
trials <- read.csv("project_data/trials.csv")
spikes <- read.csv("project_data/spikes_seg2_speaker_array_sound.csv")


cluster_type <- c("good", "mua", "noise") 
all_cluster_types <- data.frame()
for (x in cluster_type) { #make for loop for every "x" cluster
clusters_x <- clusters[clusters$group == x, ] 
spikes_x <- spikes[spikes$unit %in% clusters_x$cluster_id, ]

relative_spikes <- c() #Same for loop from previous figure
for (i in 1:1170) {
trial_onset <- trials$ttl_time_s[i]
in_window <- spikes_x$time_s >= trial_onset & spikes_x$time_s < trial_onset + 1.0
relative_spikes <- c(relative_spikes, (spikes_x$time_s[in_window] - trial_onset) * 1000)}

counts <- table(floor(relative_spikes / 5)) # number of spikes in each 5 ms bin
one_cluster_type <- data.frame(time_ms = as.numeric(names(counts)) * 5, # start time of each bin in ms
spikes_per_cluster = as.numeric(counts) / nrow(clusters_x), # divide by number of clusters per cluster type
group = x) # label the rows with teh clusters
all_cluster_types <- rbind(all_cluster_types, one_cluster_type)} #add all clusters to one table
     
ggplot(all_cluster_types, aes(x = time_ms, y = spikes_per_cluster, color = group)) +
geom_point() +
geom_line() +
labs(x = "Time After Stimulus Onset (ms)", y = "Spikes per Cluster (5ms Bins)", color = "Cluster Type", title = "Spikes After Stimulus Onset: Good vs MUA vs Noise") +
theme_minimal() 
```

![](images/paste-1.png)

6.  **Regression Model:** A simple linear regression model that compares change in activity of the neuron right after stimulus onset (0-100ms) compared to baseline activity (700-1000ms post stimulus onset). The linear model regression shows that neurons that have a high baseline activity also tend to have high evoked activity (as we would expect in a long recording with 1170 auditory trials). The geom_point line plots out the neurons that are both increasing, decreasing and not changing activity with arbitrary cutoffs. In the final project, I will be using a parameter-free ZETA test to actually find the auditory-responsive neurons.

    ```{r}
    library(ggplot2)
    clusters <- read.csv("project_data/cluster_info.csv")
    trials <- read.csv("project_data/trials.csv")
    spikes <- read.csv("project_data/spikes_seg2_speaker_array_sound.csv")
    clusters_good <- clusters[clusters$group == "good", ]
    spikes_good <- spikes[spikes$unit %in% clusters_good$cluster_id, ]

    n_per_unit <- table(spikes_good$unit)
    unit_ids <- as.integer(names(n_per_unit)[n_per_unit >= 100]) #only choose neurons that have at least 100 spikes during the whole session

    neurons <- data.frame(cluster_id = unit_ids, spont_hz = 0, evoked_hz = 0) #keep running total of spontaneous and evoked activity in hz

    for (x in seq_along(unit_ids)) { # each neuron
    spikes_x <- spikes_good$time_s[spikes_good$unit == unit_ids[x]]
    evoked <- 0
    spont <- 0
    for (i in 1:1170) {
    trial_onset <- trials$ttl_time_s[i]
    evoked <- evoked + sum(spikes_x >= trial_onset & spikes_x < trial_onset + 0.1) # evoked spikes are spikes that happened 0-100ms after onset of trial
    spont <- spont + sum(spikes_x >= trial_onset + 0.7 & spikes_x < trial_onset + 1.0)
    } #spontaneous (or baseline) rate is classfied as the end of the inter-trial interval of 1000ms (700-1000ms window)
    neurons$evoked_hz[x] <- evoked / (1170 * 0.1) # spike rate in hz
    neurons$spont_hz[x] <- spont / (1170 * 0.3)
    }

    fit <- lm(evoked_hz ~ spont_hz, data = neurons) #fit linear regression to see difference in evoked vs spontaneous activity
    summary(fit)

    neurons$change_hz <- neurons$evoked_hz - neurons$spont_hz
    neurons$response <- ifelse(neurons$change_hz > 1, "Increase",
    ifelse(neurons$change_hz < -1, "Decrease", "Little change"))
    table(neurons$response)

    ggplot(neurons, aes(x = spont_hz, y = evoked_hz, color = response)) +
    geom_point() + 
    labs(x = "Baseline Firing Rate", y = "Evoked Firing Rate", color = "Change in firing", title = "Change in Neuron Firing After Stimulus Onset") +
    theme_minimal()
    ```
